newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn's gold plan earmarked for parliament soon.
newsitem.headline: Bonn's gold plan earmarked for parliament soon.

text.p: Bonn's plan to revalue Germany's central bank reserves will be put to parliament in early June and could, if approved, help curb debts and help smooth entry into Europe's planned currency union.
Although the Bundesbank rejected Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans to revalue about 95 million ounces of gold reserves, the government made clear it intends to go ahead with the plan.
The next step will be for the Finance Ministry to introduce appropriate legislation to change the Bundesbank law, under which reserves are valued at historic lows.
This is expected on June 5 and the law could be approved by mid-June.
The Bundesbank's gold reserves are currently valued at 13.7 billion marks ($8.1 billion), far below the estimated market value of 57 billion marks.
By unlocking hidden reserve value, the government hopes to receive a sizable transfer of funds this year which could be used to redeem outstanding debt amassed during unification.
Analysts are split over whether the changes will be passed in June, particularly since the Bundesbank's strongly worded objection has galvanised public opinion.
Should it go ahead, however, the Bundesbank would be asked to revalue its reserves and hand a portion to Bonn.

Analysts predict the new valuation would still need to be some 30 percent below market value in order to ensure that if prices in gold drop, or currency values change, the Bundesbank would not suddenly face a loss on its books.
Such a move could still unlock about 20 billion marks in reserves and Bonn could receive some 10-12 billion of that amount this year, analysts said.
The Bundesbank traditionally transfers a portion of its annual profits to Bonn, and this year's transfer occurred in April.
Analysts said more tough talks would take place between Bonn and the central bank before agreement may be reached on a transfer.
Asked whether the Bundesbank could still envision any transfer this year, council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick told Reuters, "From our point of view there will not be any transfer at all."

If, however, a deal is reached, economists said a transfer could help cut the budget deficit by two-tenths of a percentage point, putting Germany's deficit -- which was 3.8 percent of GDP last year -- at or under the Maastricht Treaty's three percent target.
While there has been some controversy over how such a transfer could help Germany qualify for monetary union, several economists have said the move could effectively pare the deficit.
Bonn said it would use the transfer to redeem debt, which would free up other funds normally used to reduce such dues, to reduce the budget deficit.
But this still leaves open the question of whether the European Commission would approve such measures, economists said.
If the law is pushed through by mid June, an interim Bundesbank balance sheet could be drawn up fairly quickly, leaving Bonn free to receive the controversial transfer as early the summer.

Should the deal fail, analysts said the government could be substantially weakened. The current plans have already fanned public outrage and analysts said that in an extreme case a vote of confidence could be called.

On the other hand, they note the current situation cannot be directly compared with events that toppled Chancellor Helmut Kohl's predecessor, Helmut Schmidt, as the junior coalition partner Free Democrats are unlikely to pull out of the government.

While the central bank could be outraged if Bonn attempts to steamroll their opposition to Waigel's plan, analysts said Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer might stop short of stepping down, fearing Bonn might try to appoint a successor who would throw central bank independence to the wind.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($ = 1.701 German Marks)
